newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Moldova faces race against time on economic reform.
newsitem.headline: Moldova faces race against time on economic reform.

text.p: Moldova President Petru Lucinschi, celebrating 100 days in office on Friday, says the former Soviet republic is in a race against time to push through reforms needed to pull it out of economic crisis.
Lucinschi, a former Communist Party bureaucrat in Moscow, also says Moldova is on the right track but adds that much will depend on the decisions it takes on reforms in the next three months.
"We have no time for discussion...We have three months to stop the crisis and go ahead with reforms", he told a government meeting this week.
Lucinschi, 57, was elected last December after a campaign advocating closer ties with Moscow. He defeated his predecessor as president, pro-Romanian Mircea Snegur.

Lucinschi campaigned on a slogan of "Stability, Order, Well-being" and vowed to use his old Moscow ties to settle a six-year-old conflict between Chisinau and leaders of the separatist Dnestr region, Moldova's industrial heartland.

He appears to have kept his promise. An agreement was brokered by Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov this month under which Chisinau and Dnestr will sign a memorandum on normalising relations in Moscow on May 8.
Hundreds of people were killed in 1992 in clashes between Moldovan security forces and Dnestr rebels. The fighting was stopped by Russian troops sent to keep the peace.
Lucinschi acknowledges his achievements in the economy seem limited but says a start has been made.

"There are no wonders, especially in the economy. But there are changes. First, quarrels at the top are over", Lucinschi said in a television interview, referring to the clashes Snegur had with the parliament and government.
"We have launched cooperation between the branches of power...We have taken just the first steps to bringing stability, order and well-being to Moldova, but it is a good beginning."

Moldova's gross domestic product declined by eight percent in January to March. Its external debt grew to $1.2 billion, about 60 percent of gross domestic product and it is among the poorest countries in Europe.

"The year 1996 was lost for reforms. Until recently, Moldova was recognised as a reform leader among former Soviet republics. Today we observe stagnation of reforms", Deputy Prime Minister Ion Gutu said.
Lucinschi said: "We beleived we had reached the bottom in 1994, but we continue to fall."

The International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, Moldova's largest donors, have delayed several loans to Moldova to urge the government to speed up privatisation, reform of the tax and pension systems and changes in the energy sector.
Snegur, now an opposition leader, said the outlook would be bleak until a new reformist parliament was elected.
"1997 is lost for reforms," he said.
A parliamentary election is due early next year. Until then, deputies will be wary of passing unpopular measures which could damage their chances of being re-elected.
Parliament has adopted few of about 40 draft laws Lucinschi proposed last month, even though he said they must be adopted quickly if Moldova's economic decline is to be halted.
Even so, he vows: "The people are in despair and expect a great deal. I promised to change life for the better in two years and I will do it."
Among the 4.3 population, the jury is still out.
"Lucinschi more or less settled the Dnestr conflict. He has started to combat crime. I get my pension on time. It is small, 82 lei ($17.80)," Yelena Vasilyeva, a 55-year-old pensioner, said.
"But what could he do in 100 days? He needs at least two or three years."
Zinaida, a 39-year-old woman selling sunflower seeds near the presidential palace, was more gloomy.
"Lucinshi has done nothing. Transportation, bread and electricity prices have gone up. The last salary I got was October's," she said.
